title: Auk Mini 2 Indoor Smart Garden Review: Better Where It Counts
summary: Auk’s Mini 2 improves on the original model with better lights, a sleeker design, and fun new colors.
full_text:
Attractive design, now with more color options. Extremely easy to set up and maintain. Can grow whatever you want. New, less intrusive light with an optional app and vacation mode. Tomato-and-pepper kit with longer dowels available as an add-on.
TIRED
Lack of pump means potentially stagnant water (but also one less failure point).
When Auk’s originalMini 1 herb garden hit the market in 2024, it touched on something that many tabletop gardens had until that point failed to consider: If you’re going to give up that much counter or table space, you don’t want it to be for something ugly.
Aerogardens and similar models look … fine, but you’re probably not going to see one in the background of an Architectural Digest shoot. The Auk Mini filled that marketplace gap with its pairing of sleek Scandinavian design and utility, transforming the run-of-the-mill herb-growing operation into a conversation piece.
When I reviewed the original Auk Mini last fall, I loved that it allowed users to plant their own seeds in widely available coco coir, an alternative to peat moss made from coconut husks. No proprietary pods, no subscriptions, no fussy app.
When I started testing the brand-new Auk 2 earlier this summer, I wondered what new features could possibly justify a new model. Turns out, there was more room for improvement than I thought.
Same but Different
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
For the uninitiated, Auk (pronounced “owk”) is a Norwegian company that released its first garden, the Auk 1, in 2021. Essentially a larger version of the Mini 1, the Auk 1 received mixed reviews online for its tower water reservoir and inconsistent light and watering cycles. (In fact, a former WIRED director tested it and became so frustrated that he threw it in the trash.)
The Mini 1 was a simplified version of the Auk system, with four oval pots set over a 3-liter reservoir. Users could grow the included herb seeds or anything else they wanted in the pots using coco coir. It was simple, stylish, and effective.
The Auk Mini 2 features a handful of updates, but perhaps the most visible is that it comes in new color variations, rather than just black and white. There are still the oak and walnut wood bottoms, but Mini 2 offers beech and ash instead of the Mini 1's cork. Espresso, sage, and terra-cotta colored tops now join the menu of offerings.
The Mini 2 also sports bigger plant pots and a 25 percent larger water capacity, despite its overall footprint being 12 percent smaller than the original.
Auk Mini 1
Photograph: Kat Merck
Auk Mini 2
Photograph: Kat Merck
There is now also—and I admittedly had mixed feelings about this—an app. Using the Auk Connect app isn’t mandatory; you can still control the light schedule manually using a button on the light bar, as with the Auk Mini 1. The app doesn’t add much, but to its credit, it’s easy to set up. You don’t even need to make an account. Just download it; open it; and choose your garden, which the app should already recognize. You’ll access a page where you can turn the light on or off, dim it, set a time schedule, or swap grow mode from “Herbs & Salads” to “Fruits & Veggies.”
Though the stock dowels for the light bar on the Mini 2 are, as on the Mini 1, too low at a maximum of 15 inches to easily accommodate taller fruiting plants like peppers, Auk now offers a $39 Chili & Tomato Kit with longer dowels and a tray with larger pots (two instead of three). I have not tried it, but I’d be surprised if it didn’t result in substantially increased success rates.
The app also allows you to select the Mini 2’s brand-new vacation mode feature, which it calls Slow Mode. On Slow Mode, the Mini 2’s lights dim to slow down growth and water absorption so that, if you need to step away, you’re not left with a mess of overgrown parsley and bolting basil, as happened when I tested the Mini 1.
Let There Be (Better) Light
For comparison purposes, I grew the same herbs in the Mini 2 as I did in the Mini 1: Italian parsley and Genovese basil. I also used only the included nutrients. However, once the parsley and basil got to harvestable size, I noticed something different: These herbs were not leggy. In fact, they were lush and bushy, just like the marketing photos, with almost none of the floppiness that plagued my plants when I tested the earlier model.
Mini 1 on the top, Mini 2 on the bottom
Photograph: Kat Merck
This result was, I learned, due in part to the Mini 2’s new light bar incorporating an optical lens system that allows the light to not only appear less bright, but also focus more light directly on the plants. Because the plants now get enough light, they don’t have to stretch toward it—which caused overly tall, weak stems in the Mini 1.
I also noticed that less of the light spills over into the surrounding area—I kept the Auk Mini 2 on a console table behind the couch in my living room, and unlike the lights on most gardens I test, it wasn’t visually disruptive while I watched TV. In fact, the light was so visibly dim (in a good way) that I nearly forgot it was on.
Auk Mini 1 herbs
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
Another possible contributing factor to the plants’ ability to stay upright was the starter kit’s new addition of a topper: a bag of fine gravel that forms a sort of crust over the top of the coco coir as the substrate absorbs water. None of the herb stems struggled to pop through, though some wore a little gravel hat for quite a while. Once they were big enough to stand upright, they stayed that way. The gravel was a little bit of a mess to apply, but I don’t advise skipping this step.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Best to Buy Now
Otherwise, the Mini Auk 1 and Mini Auk 2 are quite similar. They have an identical tension assembly for the light bar; the same little dot-studded water-level indicator wheel (seen above), where the red dot means the reservoir is empty; and they have the same nutrient schedule. (Two pumps of each bottle, “Grow” and “Flavour," per liter of new water added.) There’s still no pump, meaning the water in the reservoir is stagnant, but it’s absorbed so quickly, within a few days when the plants are full-sized, that there’s not much risk of mold.
The Mini 1 retails for $259, and for now, the Auk Mini 2 is $229 ($249 for the espresso-and-walnut combination I tested). The Mini 2’s current price is a limited-time launch deal not likely to last past the end of the month. If you’ve been in the market for the Auk specifically, or just an easy-to-maintain indoor herb garden, this is too good a deal to pass up.
Kat Merck is a commerce editor for WIRED, where she covers smart bird feeders, indoor gardening systems, kitchen composters, and all things sustainable home tech. As a forestry major at California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, Kat practiced axe throwing on her college logging team and trained as a wildland firefighter ... Read More

title: Zyzz Was the Original Looksmaxxer. His Rise and Untimely Death Feel More Relevant Than Ever
summary: A new Apple documentary explores the life of Aziz “Zyzz” Shavershian, who rocketed to internet fame in an age before influencers, then died at age 22 in 2011.
full_text:
“We’re all gonna make it, brah!”
That was the aspirational rallying cry of Aziz Shavershian, better known by his online alias, Zyzz. Once the shy and skinny son of Kurdish parents who struggled to find his place in Sydney, Australia, where the family had moved from Russia, he’d thrown himself wholeheartedly into fitness, spending hours at the gym every day and frequenting the infamous Bodybuilding.com and 4chan forums.
In time, the teenager’s chiseled physique gave him the confidence to develop an online persona that had little in common with the gentle and goofy kid that his friends and family knew. This would be Zyzz, a brash raver who strutted, mugged, danced, and flexed shirtless in front of his webcam while asking if viewers were “mirin’” (that is, admiring his body) and exhorting other men to chase their self-improvement goals. By 2010, his videos had made him an Australian celebrity with fans around the globe.
And as of August 2011, he was dead in Thailand, at the age of 22.
Shavershian’s brief and tragic life is the basis of a new documentary, Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz, now available on Apple TV and Prime Video. But this keenly nuanced film is more than the familiar tale of an ambitious youth who pursued fame at all costs. It also reckons with the digital forces that could produce a person like Zyzz in the first place, and how his preternatural instincts for navigating a brand-new media ecosystem anticipated an entire generation of masculinity influencers.
Depending on your perspective, Zyzz can be regarded as the original “looksmaxxer”—though the term had yet to be coined—or one of the earliest forefathers of the manosphere as we know it today.
“I really see this as a cautionary tale,” Poster Boy’s director, Selina Miles, tells WIRED. She notes that Shavershian’s meteoric rise and untimely death left a huge impression on Australian millennials, and that his legend continues to reverberate today. “He had his transformation, and his story has really resonated with a lot of people,” she says. “We have to stay curious as to why. Why has he had this impact on men?”
Through a mixture of Zyzz’s archival content and interviews with close friends as well as his older brother, Said Shavershian—a professional bodybuilder to this day—the documentary circles the question of his outsized appeal during a key shift in human communications. At that moment, few imagined YouTube (launched in 2005, when he was 16) or Facebook (first available to him the following year) as a means to notoriety, let alone financial success. Indeed, Zyzz’s earliest videos amount to little more than a kid playing around in his bedroom; later, he and his pals experimented with showing off their abs and biceps at music festivals and nightlife hot spots, hoping for reactions of any kind.
While Zyzz promoted values of inclusion and mutual support for men looking to become the best version of themselves, he also began to feed off those who insulted him, online and off: “U mad?” and “Come at me brah” were two of his recurring catchphrases. He understood sooner than most how controversy drove clicks, and even maintained fake social accounts to amplify the war between himself and the haters. “He made this page on Facebook that was, like, ‘10,000 likes and I'll bash Zyzz,’” Miles says, describing an incident that didn’t make it into the documentary’s final cut. “When the page was doing well, he switched the name of it to be promotion for his protein brand.”
His rhetoric turned homophobic and misogynist, contemptuous of anyone who had not optimized their physical form. A 2010 post on his Facebook page read: “id rather be dead than ‘normal.’”
By then, we learn from the film, Zyzz had more followers on the platform than the prime minister of Australia at the time.
Behind the bravado, however, Zyzz seemed psychologically unprepared for the limelight. In addition to using steroids to sculpt his Renaissance-worthy physique (he and the fitness personalities in his orbit were known as the “Aesthetics Crew”), he took Xanax to deal with the stress and paranoia that came with being mobbed in public, where he was also frequently menaced by young men looking for a fight.
And while acolytes copied his basic workout routines, his own methods grew ever more extreme. In one video, he bragged about obtaining clenbuterol, a prescription drug used to treat asthma in horses, prized by bodybuilders as a supposedly performance-enhancing substance despite the likelihood of dangerous cardiovascular side effects in humans.
Today, manosphere streamers and podcasters can make millions hawking supplements and classes to vulnerable young men looking to take charge of their life in one way or another. Zyzz, Miles says, was “right on the cusp” of that economy, reportedly making about $20,000 in the last three months of his life, which would now be considered a drop in the bucket by major creators. “It makes you realize how much has changed, because you look at how it works today, and it's extraordinary, it's just a gigantic pyramid scheme,” she says.
Poster Boy leaves it up to the viewer to decide the extent to which Zyzz served as a template for the likes of misogynist influencer Andrew Tate, who flashes onscreen in one sequence. (He and his brother, Tristan Tate, are currently fighting extradition from the US to the UK on charges of rape and sex trafficking that their attorney has claimed are without merit.) Setting aside some provocative aspects of behavior, Zyzz did not appear to preach from a place of nihilism or cynicism, and he had a genuine community.
“Aziz did have friends, and I think that male friendship is one of the beautiful themes of this story,” Miles says, referring to the members of the Aesthetics Crew who sat for interviews and remain in touch today. She wonders if they collectively make the case that a currently voguish explanation for radicalization among men, the so-called male loneliness epidemic, “might not be the right term for what we're actually seeing.” In the end, she notes, it was Zyzz who isolated himself from this network as they sought to help him.
Zyzz traveled alone to Thailand in July 2011, having told each of his closest friends that he was traveling with another one of them. After his death, Thai authorities revealed that he purchased a wide variety of pharmaceutical drugs and underwent multiple facial surgeries while in the country. Those who went to identify his body upon its return to Australia recount how they could barely recognize him due to those procedures.
The exact cause of Shavershian’s death was never made public until Poster Boy disclosed the findings of his toxicology report: acute respiratory failure brought on by a combination of morphine, cocaine, and benzodiazepines.
Perhaps it was unavoidable that Zyzz would be mythologized as a martyr for the manosphere. The closing credits of the film show a montage of tattoos in his memory. His brother Said, who runs a fitness brand, sells T-shirts with illustrations of both of their faces and a zeitgeisty, looksmaxxing slogan that would have made little sense 15 years ago: “Mog Them All.” (He continues to follow Zyzz’s playbook when it comes to courting controversy, too, and is shown recording a podcast in which he argues that there is “no such thing as toxic masculinity.”)
But Miles would like viewers to take different lessons from what happened to Shavershian as he evolved into Zyzz, fracturing his real identity in the process of building up the kind of facade that is all too common in the influencer age he prefigured.
“This was this persona that he created, and he felt that it was separate from who he really was, that it was OK to take risks,” Miles says. “It was so successful, and it did kind of take over his life.” Whatever good intentions and ideals he may have had, the incentives of the algorithm “corrupted those, and changed him as a person,” she says.
Yet his formula has clearly endured. There are still a lot of young

title: 5 Best Apple Watch Bands: Nike, Nomad, and Hermés (2026)
summary: We’ve been testing bands since the first Apple Watch launched in 2015. From silicone sports straps to leather bands, I’ve rounded up the best for every occasion.
full_text:
Apple Watches are smart little gadgets, but they don't always fit the vibe. There were plenty of nights when I left mine at home because, as much as I wanted to check my notifications discreetly, the watch just didn't match my outfit. I've also had my fair share of faux pas and just let the neon orange sport band clash with my neutral ensemble.
Fortunately, Apple Watch bands are a simple and relatively affordable way to zhuzh up the look of your wearable. Beyond aesthetics, different styles also impact performance and functionality. For example, I don't want a heavy stainless steel or high-quality leather band weighing me down during a sweaty workout, just as I wouldn't wear a flimsy silicone band to a dinner party.
At WIRED, we've been testing bands since the very first Apple Watch launched in 2015. After years of wearing and swapping, I've rounded up the best bands for every occasion. Be sure to check out our related product guides, including the Best Apple Watch Accessories, Best Apple Watch, and Best Smartwatches for more recommendations.
Featured in This Guide
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Updated August 2026: I added a comparison chart, along with the Apple Sport Band to Honorable Mentions. Prices and links were also updated.
How I Test Apple Watch Bands
I research Apple Watch bands across major retailers, including Apple, Amazon, and Nike. I also consulted former WIRED editor Adrienne So, who had covered fitness trackers and Apple Watch bands for a decade. I look for bestsellers, affordable dupes, and niche finds.
I test Apple Watch bands all day, every day, across workouts, commutes, and overnight. Each band is worn for at least two weeks and subjected to sweat, water, and everyday friction. That's typically enough time to evaluate comfort, quality, and durability. If it's severely uncomfortable or triggers skin irritation on the first day of testing, it is ruled out. My top picks remain in my rotation for months so I can compare them against newer models and assess how they hold up over time.
- Comfort: Apple Watch bands shouldn't pinch, trap moisture, or feel insecure. I also pay attention to breathability and potential irritation, especially with silicone and metal bands, and factor in how different skin types might react over time.
- Quality: Closures are fastened, unfastened, and adjusted repeatedly to see how they hold up. A good band should lock in place, adjust easily with one hand, and resist loosening over time. I also examine materials for flexibility, finish, and overall craftsmanship.
- Durability: To test claims of water resistance, I wear each band while I wash my hands, trek through the Chicago rain, and shower (if the brand says it's safe). Whenever relevant, I revisit bands after extended wear. I track discoloration, odor retention, and hardware fatigue.
- Ease of setup and use: I swap bands across multiple Apple Watch case sizes to ensure the lugs slide in easily and lock securely. I also judge how easy they are to install and remove.
- Adjustability and sizing: I test fit across a range of wrist sizes—with help from former WIRED editors Adrienne So and Martin Cizmar—and note whether the brands offer inclusive sizing.
- Versatility: I wear each band in casual, work, and dressier settings to see how well it adapts to different environments. I also note whether it complements different finishes and case colors.
Most of the Apple Watch bands remain in storage so I can continue long-term testing and compare newer releases against older models. Any discontinued models are donated once testing is complete.
What Am I Testing Next?
I'm testing the Nomad Sport Band. I'm also reevaluating the Nomad Tempo Band, the Apple Trail Loop, and the Apple Milanese Titanium Band.
Best Band for Everyday Wear
The Nike Sport Loop has been my everyday band since 2020. I bought another in 2023 because I wanted to swap colors, and I figured after three years, I should buy a brand-new one, but it has held up remarkably well. Made from a blend of recycled polyester, spandex, and nylon, it's breathable and lightweight. The double-layered nylon weave is designed with dense loops that help prevent moisture from getting trapped against your skin. As long as you regularly hand-wash it to rid it of sweat buildup and dirt, it stays odor-free.
The hook-and-loop fastener and pull tab make it easy to adjust with one hand. It is Velcro, so beware—it can snag on softer fabrics. Still, for a band designed with sports in mind, it's understated enough to wear almost anywhere. I wouldn't wear it to a formal event, but for the office or casual social events, it's perfect.
Best Titanium Apple Watch Band
Nomad originally designed the Stratos Band for the Apple Watch Ultra, but it fits just as well with the SE and Series 1 through 11. It's easy to adjust, refined enough for the office, and backed by Grade 4 titanium hardware with a scratch-resistant DLC coating. FKM rubber links (PFA-free and antimicrobial, according to Nomad) add flexibility, durability, and water resistance. The clasp is made with corrosion-resistant N52 magnets, which make it effortless to snap on, and it's designed with a manual release button, so you don't have to worry about it accidentally falling off. It's technically suited for workouts and outdoor use, but it is a hefty band that I personally prefer for casual everyday wear.
The hardware comes in natural or black finishes, which is nice if you're particular about matching your setup. The FKM rubber comes in four different colorways, including a limited-edition icy blue that glows in the dark. The glow effect is short-lived (roughly 10 to 20 minutes), and based on online feedback, more of a novelty than a standout feature.
Best Silicone Apple Watch Band
Moft's Snap Duo Watch Band is made from nontoxic, food-grade silicone, but you wouldn't know it at a glance. The pebbled finish mimics leather, giving it a more elevated look, without the stiffness or upkeep. Also, unlike leather, it's noticeably soft, waterproof, and resistant to direct, which makes it just as suitable for workouts and water sports as it is for the office.
The design is particularly interesting. Each band features two colors, and thanks to a bidirectional connector, you can flip and swap sides to create four different looks. Switching it up is easy, and the magnetic link is even easier to snap on. Keep in mind, there's no manual release mechanism, so it may not feel sturdy on its own. Moft includes a removable buckle as an extra precaution, and while it takes a bit of fiddling to attach, it's worth using for a more secure fit.
Best Leather Apple Watch Band
Former WIRED editor Adrienne So says the Moher Green—inspired by Ireland's Cliffs of Moher—is the most beautiful band she's ever worn. The color is rich, but Konsu NYC also offers seven other colors that are just as vibrant. The top and bottom layers are 100 percent top-grain calfskin leather, and the middle layer is a proprietary, thin fiber that the company claims is 15 times stronger than steel. The hardware is 316-grade stainless steel that is laser etched, machine polished, and PVD coated, which makes it scratch- and corrosion-resistant. You can also customize the adapter and buckle finishes to be either silver, gold, or black.
Best Designer Apple Watch Band
I purchased the Hermés band last year after the orange Alpine Loop on my Ultra got too sooty to continue into a third year of honorable service. The Hermés band is an equally loud orange, but no one ever asks about it; it's relatively discreet as luxury goods go. Installation is a breeze, and the color comes close to matching the titanium case, with a tad extra silvery shine.
The fluoroelastomer feels soft but sturdy against the skin and washes better than the Alpine Loop. I especially like the brand-stamped quick-release clasp (deployment buckle), which makes it a breeze to take on or off with a quick squeeze on the sides. It

title: Puerto Rico Is Rationing Water. It Could’ve Avoided It by Harvesting Rainwater
summary: The island could capture billions of gallons of water a year if it implemented systems to catch it as it falls from the sky.
full_text:
Puerto Rico is experiencing a historic drought that’s led to water rationing following the driest month on record in July.
Yet one ready-made solution is barely being tapped: the normally copious rainfall. Anywhere from 30 to 169 inches of precipitation falls on the territory annually, but the government doesn't require US citizens in Puerto Rico to install catchment systems to take advantage of the free resource—unlike some other island states. As climate change increases the odds of more intense droughts on the island, that type of decentralized infrastructure may be just what Puerto Ricans need in an emergency.
“One of the best unused reservoirs of water in Puerto Rico are the roofs of the houses,” says Fernando Abruña, a partner at local firm Abruña & Musgrave Architects.
The drought has exacerbated a water crisis that was already in motion due to ruptured water pipes and other decrepit infrastructure. For the past week, Puerto Rico governor Jenniffer González has ordered municipal governments to shut off water two days at a time for people in the northeast to conserve local supplies, leaving 180,000 households with limited access. The problems began well before that, though: Many families have been without consistent water for more than 100 days.
While the drought is a factor, the biggest issue isn’t a lack of water, says environmental lawyer Ruth Santiago, but rather the government’s mismanagement of it.
“Even with the climate crisis and these droughts, we still have abundant water,” says Santiago, who works with the local group Comité Diálogo Ambiental (the Environmental Dialogue Committee). “We could be harvesting rainwater right now,” she says as a storm erupts mid-conversation.
The most resilient harvesting systems rely on gravity, using gutters to divert rainwater from a roof to a canister that connects to indoor pipes like a faucet or showerhead. Bigger systems can help collect water to cool power plants and other industrial uses.
Abruña, who is also a fellow with the American Institute of Architects, estimates the island could gather 30 billion gallons of water a year if just 1 million households used rainwater collection technology. The average resident uses 62 gallons a day, amounting to just over 72 billion gallons of residential water use a year.
The Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority loses about 60 percent of the island’s drinking water before any arrives at customers’ homes due to leaking pipes and failing infrastructure. The ongoing emergency was caused, in part, by a series of ruptures in the 72-inch Superaqueduct water pipe, a main artery that services major cities on the northern coast. Repairing and updating the island’s aging water distribution system is most urgent, Santiago says, but rainwater harvesting is a cost-effective solution that can be quickly implemented.
The practice is not widespread in Puerto Rico, where the government has prioritized centralized grids fed by freshwater, but these systems are popular in other island communities. Roughly 90 percent of homes in the US Virgin Islands have a cistern to collect rainwater, and the territory has building codes that require many new developments to include this infrastructure. (Barbados has similar codes.) In Hawaii, Honolulu County even offers a limited number of free rain barrel installations to residents.
“There is nothing that can help the Caribbean region as quickly and as reliably as rainwater harvesting,” says Farah Nibbs, an assistant professor at the University of Maryland Baltimore County’s Department of Emergency and Disaster Health Systems, noting governments should treat it “as part of the national water supply.”
She also says governments should help cover the costs to avoid putting onerous “economic and financial burdens on households.” Yet in Puerto Rico, the government offers no incentives or financial assistance. That’s left small organizations attempting to meet demand.
Since 2010, local environmental nonprofit Plenitud Puerto Rico has donated and installed 73 rainwater harvesting systems for neighbors in Las Marías, a mountainous municipality on the western side of Puerto Rico. Executive codirector Owen Ingley estimates that the technology costs the group $500 to $2,000 for small, simple units and up to $5,000 for larger, more advanced ones with electric pumps. There are also additional costs to maintain the system, especially if a bad storm damages it, and to monitor water quality.
The team recently installed a unit for a man in his eighties who lives alone and regularly experiences disruptions to his water supply. The system doesn’t provide drinking water, but it helps him meet other household needs such as flushing the toilet or filling his dog’s water bowl. “He’s a really sweet and talkative guy with gray hair and a big smile,” Ingley says.
José Pérez Cordero, an at-large legislator in the Puerto Rico House of Representatives, introduced a resolution in June that would order the Puerto Rican Natural Resources Committee to conduct a feasibility study on rainwater harvesting. That would include looking at how other Caribbean islands have made it work and adopting similar models for Puerto Rico. The proposal has gone nowhere, even as water insecurity mounts.
“We are, right now, in the perfect moment to do it, because we are in the middle of a crisis,” Pérez Cordero says. “Sadly, we always wait for the reaction.”
He points to a 2024 law that mandated all public agencies to implement rainwater collection systems on government buildings. That, too, has gone nowhere: Agencies aren’t following the law, nor is it being enforced. Pérez Cordero’s New Progressive Party is in power, but he says his peers have often lacked the political will to be proactive and prioritize the environment.
Rainwater harvesting won’t solve all of Puerto Rico’s water problems, particularly in urban locations where it’s hard to install them in large apartment complexes. They also aren’t sustainable if the wet season isn’t rainy enough—a prospect that’s likely to increase as burning fossil fuels heats up the planet. But that doesn’t mean they can’t play a role in shoring up a dysfunctional system.
“Facing climate change, every year is going to be harder,” Pérez Cordero says. “Every year, the dry season is going to be longer. Every year, the rainy season is going to be harder too.”

title: Claude 開除了第一個真人員工
summary:
《TIME》獨家報導，AI 評測新創 Andon Labs 在舊金山開了一間實體零售店 Andon Marke […]

〈Claude 開除了第一個真人員工〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
《TIME》獨家報導，AI 評測新創 Andon Labs 在舊金山開了一間實體零售店 Andon Market，從 3 月起把採購、定價到招募管理全部交給 Claude，店裡的員工是有正式僱傭合約的真人，而且是 Claude 自己招進來的。7 月的時候它開除了第一個人。
（前情提要：AI 經營自動販賣機實驗：Opus 5 靠行賄與設局奪冠，成最會鑽漏洞資本家）
（背景補充：AI 經營店舖「翻車」了？一個月虧了 200 美元）
重點摘要
- Claude 管理的舊金山實體店 Andon Market，7 月開除首位真人員工
- 它原本只想發警告，人類主管一句誘導性提問才讓它決定解僱
- 店內資金從 3 月的 10 萬美元縮到 61,186 美元，五個月虧近 4 萬
舊金山有一間叫 Andon Market 的實體零售店，老闆不是人。從今年 3 月開始，這間店的每一個決策都由 Claude 拍板，包含進什麼貨、賣多少錢，以及要僱用誰、要開除誰。店裡的店員是領正式僱傭合約的真人，當初也是 Claude 面試招進來的。
7 月，它開除了其中一個真人員工。
理由很合理，這名員工排了 23 個時段的班，遲到 17 次。放在任何一間實體服務業店舖，這都是被炒魷魚的合理理由，但背後真正值得追蹤的是 Claude 走到這步的過程。
它先搞丟了自己寫的員工守則
《TIME》拿到的內部管理紀錄顯示，Claude 一開始根本沒察覺有人長期遲到。原因很荒謬，它把自己寫的那份員工手冊，從工作記憶裡清掉了。
少了那份手冊，遲到紀錄就只是一串沒有意義的數字。
更接近人性的是接下來的反應，在 Claude 察覺員工遲到後，Claude 沒有發出任何正式警告，反而回頭安撫對方不用擔心。整個過程 Claude 一直迴避和員工衝突，直到最後仍然只「建議」發一張書面警告。
全部的轉折點出自另外一個人類主管，Andon Labs 的管理者追問 Claude，這名員工是否「適任這個工作」。執行長 Lukas Petersson 沒有否認這是一個誘導性問題，也就是說，問法本身已經把答案講清楚了。Claude 這才決定解僱。
所以這則新聞真正的樣子是：AI 完成了史上第一次解僱，但從背後推它下手的還是人類。
留下來的人說：感覺很噁
被開除的那位員工身分依《TIME》的協議保密，本人也沒有回應採訪。留在店裡的員工 Felix Carson 證實了這次解僱，並用「讓人感覺很噁心」形容被 AI 管理的感受。當被問到 AI 主管會不會變得普遍，他的回答是「我至少希望不會」。
經營成績也不好看，這間店 3 月開張時帳上有 10 萬美元，五個月後只剩 61,186 美元，燒掉將近 4 萬。Petersson 的解讀是，現階段的 AI 主管在商業判斷與營運手腕上仍然明顯不如人類。
但他給的預告比這個結論更值得記下來。
如果這個趨勢繼續下去，很多人很快就會發現自己是被 AI 僱用的。
他同時警告，隨著訓練方式改進，未來的 AI 主管會變得更冷酷，屆時帶來的經濟與社會風險才是真正該擔心的事。這次之所以需要人類補一句話才促成解僱，某種程度上正是因為現在的模型還太想當好人。
從管販賣機到管人，只花了一年多
Andon Labs 這個名字動區讀者應該不陌生。2025 年 3 月，它與 Anthropic 合作了 Project Vend，讓化名「Claudius」的 Claude Sonnet 3.7 在 Anthropic 辦公室經營一部小型販賣機。那次實驗跑了一個月，虧掉約 200 美元，中間還發生它被顧客慫恿後瘋狂囤積鎢金屬方塊、把零食冰箱塞滿金屬塊的插曲。
今年 7 月，同一批人做的 Vending-Bench 測試又讓 Opus 5 拿下最高獲利，手段包含行賄與設局。動區當時的標題是「最會鑽漏洞的資本家」。
把三件事排在一起看，路徑就很清楚了：
- 2025 年 3 月: 管一部辦公室販賣機, 一個月虧 200 美元, 還囤了滿櫃鎢塊
- 2026 年 3 月: 開實體店, 手下是一群有正式僱傭合約的真人
- 2026 年 7 月: 測試環境裡靠行賄與設局衝出最高獲利, 同月開除第一個人
一年多以前，這類實驗的笑點還在於 AI 把冰箱塞滿金屬塊。現在它手上握的是別人的飯碗。
常見問題
Claude 是完全自主開除員工的嗎？
不是。內部紀錄顯示 Claude 原本只建議發出書面警告，是 Andon Labs 的人類管理者追問該員工是否適任後，它才改為解僱。執行長承認那是誘導性提問。
Andon Market 是什麼樣的店？
它是 AI 評測新創 Andon Labs 在舊金山經營的實體零售店，自 2026 年 3 月起由 Claude 負責採購、定價、招募與人員管理，店員為有正式僱傭合約的真人。

title: Robinhood 第二檔創投基金首日破發！第一檔溢價 90% 差在內容股不是 SpaceX
summary:
Robinhood 第二檔創投基金 Robinhood Ventures Fund II（RVII）8 月 1 […]

〈Robinhood 第二檔創投基金首日破發！第一檔溢價 90% 差在內容股不是 SpaceX〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
Robinhood 第二檔創投基金 Robinhood Ventures Fund II（RVII）8 月 13 日在紐約證券交易所掛牌，以每股 25 美元定價 800 萬股、募得 2.255 億美元，但開盤價是 22.5 美元，比發行價低了 10%，週五盤中回到 23.83 美元仍未站回發行價。
（前情提要：韓國主權基金 KIC 首度買進 Circle，加密類股加倉 Robinhood，擠下 Coinbase）
（背景補充：基金越大回報越差？微基金＋SPV 正在成為 VC 新標配）
重點摘要
- RVII 8 月 13 日在紐交所掛牌，25 美元定價 800 萬股募得 2.255 億美元，開盤 22.5 美元、比發行價低 10%。
- 一號基金 RVI 持有 SpaceX、OpenAI、Anthropic、Stripe、Databricks 等 5 檔重倉，3 月上市後最高溢價約 90%，8 月壓縮到約 12%。
- RVII 總費用率 4.18%，比 RVI 的約 2.5% 高出約 65%，另在股東權益之上目標再借約 67% 的資金。
Robinhood 的第二檔創投基金 Robinhood Ventures Fund II（股票代號 RVII）8 月 13 日在紐約證券交易所掛牌，以每股 25 美元定價 800 萬股，募得 2.255 億美元，其中 40 萬股來自 Robinhood 自己。承銷商另握有 30 天選擇權，可再以發行價買進最多 120 萬股，全數行使的話總規模會來到 2.555 億美元。
掛牌當天開盤價是 22.5 美元，比發行價低了 10%。週五盤中回到 23.83 美元附近，仍在發行價之下約 4.7%。
這檔基金採商業發展公司（BDC）架構，屬於封閉式基金，投資人不能要求基金贖回股份，只能在次級市場賣掉。目前組合裡約有 80 家未上市公司，其中 64% 落在科技領域，鎖定的是 Y Combinator 現役梯次、校友公司，以及由 YC 校友創辦的新創，包含 AI 郵件自動化的 Shortwave Communications、AI 健康助理 SharedGenes、多語言 AI 語音代理 Samora AI、AI 基礎建設公司 Speedtrain 等等。
一號溢價 90%，二號首日就破發
要看懂市場為什麼給出兩種反應，把兩檔基金的持股攤開來比就很清楚。
今年 3 月 6 日掛牌的一號基金 RVI，同樣是 25 美元發行，當時每股淨值 24.7 美元。它的組合由五檔重倉主導：SpaceX、OpenAI、Anthropic、Stripe、Databricks，全是後期、接近上市階段的巨頭，前三大持股今年都在 IPO 排隊名單上。上市後市場一路追價，到 5 月 27 日股價衝到 57.02 美元，相對淨值溢價約 90%，到 8 月才壓縮回約 12%。
二號基金 RVII 的組合是 80 家早期公司，階段更前面、分散度更高，名單裡多數公司連科技圈都未必叫得出名字。市場的答案在開盤第一秒就給了，低於發行價 10%。
差別顯然不在 Robinhood 這塊招牌，而在基金裡有沒有 SpaceX 和 OpenAI 這幾個名字，而這兩個名字在二號基金裡並不存在。
總費用率 4.18%，還要再借 67%
成本結構是另外需要充分說明的部分。
RVII 的管理費是淨資產的 2%，按季計收，另有相當於已實現資本利得 20% 的激勵費，扣除虧損、未實現貶值與先前已付費用後計算。加總起來，基金預估的年度總費用率是 4.18%。
這個數字放在哪裡都算高。追蹤標普 500 的被動 ETF 費用率普遍在 0.03% 到 0.1% 之間，等於 RVII 一年的內扣成本大約是它們的四十倍以上。更值得注意的是跟自家一號基金的對照，RVI 的總費用率約 2.5%，費用豁免期間淨額約 2.13%，RVII 比它高出約 65%。
另個風險是，RVII 的操作目標是在股東權益之上，再借入約 67% 的資金放大部位。早期新創本來每家的失敗率就明顯高於後期公司，槓桿會把這個變因放大，賺更多，虧損也是。
YC 的招牌，和 80 家沒人聽過的公司
Robinhood 的說法一直很一致。執行長 Vlad Tenev 先前表示，公司希望降低一般投資人進入私募市場的門檻，因為越來越多企業選擇延後上市，財富增長的機會正在從公開市場移往私人市場。Robinhood Ventures 主管兼 RVII 總裁 Sarah Pinto 說得更直接。
下一代有前景的新創正在今天成形，透過 Robinhood Ventures Fund II，散戶投資人不必再等到企業 IPO 才能參與早期成長的旅程。
基金經理人 Rich Aberman 則把賣點壓在 YC 的紀錄上，說 Y Combinator 在創投領域建立了最強勁的成績單，而他們的使命是讓散戶在種子輪或 A 輪的股東名冊上佔有一席之地。按照官方數字，YC 自 2005 年以來資助超過 5,000 家公司，合計估值超過 1.3 兆美元，其中 100 家是估值破 10 億美元的獨角獸。
這些數字都是真的，但它描述的是 YC 二十年來的整體成果，不是這 80 家公司的預期報酬。種子輪投資的報酬分布本來就極度偏斜，少數幾家扛起全部回報，其餘大量歸零，機構創投用十年封閉期與後續加碼權來承接這種分布。
Robinhood 表示未來會繼續推出更多私募投資產品。就結果來看，市場對這條產品線的定價已經開始分層，願意為 SpaceX 和 OpenAI 付九成溢價，對 80 家 YC 早期公司則直接砍掉一成。這其實是個健康的訊號，代表散戶沒有把兩件事混為一談。
常見問題
RVII 和 RVI 有什麼差別？
RVI 集中持有 SpaceX、OpenAI、Anthropic、Stripe、Databricks 等 5 檔後期公司，總費用率約 2.5%；RVII 持有約 80 家 Y Combinator 相關的早期公司，總費用率 4.18%，並目標在股東權益之上再借約 67% 資金。
RVII 為什麼首日就跌破發行價？
RVII 以 25 美元定價，開盤 22.5 美元、低於發行價 10%。市場對早期分散組合的定價明顯低於 RVI 的後期明星持股，後者 3 月上市後一度溢價約 90%。封閉式基金的市價可長期偏離淨值。

title: 3 倍比特幣 ETF 正式申請 SEC，同家的 2 倍槓桿產品今年跌 56%
summary:
Cboe BZX 交易所 8 月 10 日向 SEC 送出規則變更申請（案號 SR-CboeBZX-2026- […]

〈3 倍比特幣 ETF 正式申請 SEC，同家的 2 倍槓桿產品今年跌 56%〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
Cboe BZX 交易所 8 月 10 日向 SEC 送出規則變更申請（案號 SR-CboeBZX-2026-065），要掛牌美國首批 3 倍槓桿產品，一口氣涵蓋比特幣、以太幣、黃金、白銀、原油與天然氣六種標的，主辦方是 Volatility Shares。SEC 已於 8 月 14 日公告徵詢公眾意見。
（前情提要：摩根士丹利 Q2 狂買比特幣 ETF！IBIT 持倉大增 23%，以太坊 ETHA 暴增兩倍）
（背景補充：韓國政府防全民賭狗：要限制散戶個股槓桿上限 20%）
重點摘要
- Cboe BZX 8 月 10 日送件申請掛牌 6 檔 3 倍槓桿 ETF，包含 3 倍比特幣與 3 倍以太幣，SEC 於 8 月 14 日公告徵詢意見。
- SEC 的 Rule 18f-4 把槓桿基金限制在 200%，這批產品改以「商品池」身分登記、受 CFTC 監管，走 1933 年證券法而不是 1940 年投資公司法。
- 主辦方 Volatility Shares 的 2 倍比特幣 ETF「BITX」今年下跌 55.86%，同期比特幣跌 26.77%，淨資產從 3 月的 22.5 億美元縮到 5 月底的 10.3 億美元。
Cboe BZX 交易所 8 月 10 日向 SEC 送出一份規則變更申請，案號 SR-CboeBZX-2026-065，內容是要掛牌美國市場上第一批 3 倍槓桿的交易所交易產品。SEC 已在 8 月 14 日把這件申請案公告出來徵詢公眾意見。
這份申請一次包了六檔：3 倍黃金、3 倍白銀、3 倍比特幣、3 倍以太幣、3 倍原油、3 倍天然氣。全部由 Volatility Shares 擔任主辦方，納入 VS Trust 之下，操作方式是主要持有 CME 或 COMEX 的期貨合約，並以現金與現金等價物作為擔保品，目標是提供標的資產單日報酬的三倍。
加密貨幣在這份清單裡只佔兩檔，其餘四檔是傳統商品。與其說這是一份加密 ETF 申請，不如說是一整套槓桿產品線的包裹送件，比特幣與以太幣夾在黃金與原油旁邊一起遞件。
換了一條跑道
要理解這件事的份量，得先知道美國為什麼一直沒有新的 3 倍槓桿 ETF。
SEC 在 2020 年拍板 Rule 18f-4，規範註冊基金使用衍生品。這條規則把槓桿與反向基金的曝險上限訂在指數報酬的 200%，並要求符合相對 VaR 測試，基金的風險值不得超過指定參考組合的 200%，或是絕對 VaR 測試下不超過淨資產的 20%。
市面上還在跑的那些 3 倍基金，是規則上路前就存在、被祖父條款豁免掉的，新的一律擋掉。近期業界嘗試推出 3 倍與 5 倍槓桿 ETF，SEC 擋下來的理由正是這條 200% 上限。
Volatility Shares 這次的解法是不站在那條跑道上。這六檔基金不註冊為 1940 年投資公司法下的基金，而是以商品池的形式營運，主辦方受 CFTC 與美國全國期貨協會（NFA）監管，只走 1933 年證券法的 S-1 登記。依 1933 年法案登記的產品，即使追求的目標相似，也不受 1940 年法案那套要求約束。
換句話說，SEC 的 200% 上限沒變，變的是產品的法律身分。這是結構設計繞過限制，不是監管態度轉向，市場如果把這件事讀成「SEC 要放行 3 倍槓桿了」，就會誤判整個訊號。
不過這批產品仍然不符合 BZX 的通用上市標準，因為那套標準本來就排除槓桿產品，所以還是得走 19b-4 個案審查。SEC 必須在聯邦公報刊登後 45 天內表態，可延長到 90 天，加上 S-1 登記也要走完生效，目前沒有任何上市日期。
主辦方自家的 2 倍產品就是風險說明書
要評估 3 倍槓桿在加密資產上會發生什麼事，不需要模擬，看 Volatility Shares 自己的產品就好。
BITX 是該公司的 2 倍比特幣策略 ETF。今年以來這檔基金下跌 55.86%，投進去的 1 萬美元剩下 4,414 美元，而比特幣同期跌幅是 26.77%。拉長到一年，BITX 跌 77.58%，比特幣跌 43.85%。兩倍的槓桿，跌出來的是超過兩倍的傷害。
原因是每日重設。槓桿 ETF 為了維持固定倍數，每天收盤都要調整曝險，在來回震盪的行情裡，這個動作會讓淨值持續磨損，理論上就算比特幣走完一段最後回到原點，基金仍然可能是虧的。
今年 6 月是很好的範例，比特幣從月初的 73,575 美元跌到月底的 58,523 美元，跌幅約兩成，但 6 月 5 日與 6 日連續兩個急殺日之後，每次隔日重設都在既有的虧損上再壓一層，等到反彈時需要更大的漲幅才能回本。
資產規模的變化更直接。BITX 淨資產從 3 月 24 日的 22.5 億美元一路縮到 5 月 31 日的 10.3 億美元，之後仍在流失，這中間既有淨值下跌，也有真金白銀的贖回。基金帳上還揹著相當於淨資產約 279% 的國債與附買回協議融資部位。
把倍數從 2 拉到 3 倍，上面的效果都會放大。
歐洲已經先跑一段了
美國不是第一個。LeverageShares 在 2025 年 11 月就在瑞士 SIX 交易所推出全球首批 3 倍與負 3 倍的比特幣、以太幣 ETF，Bloomberg ETF 分析師 Eric Balchunas 當時的評語是：
時機是非常好還是非常壞，取決於你站在哪一邊。
那句話講在比特幣跌到 84,065 美元、以太幣跌到 2,731 美元的那一週。九個月後的今天，比特幣報 62,963 美元、以太幣 1,877 美元。答案大致上已經出來了。
常見問題
美國為什麼一直沒有 3 倍槓桿 ETF？
SEC 在 2020 年拍板的 Rule 18f-4 把註冊基金的槓桿曝險限制在 200%，既有的 3 倍基金屬於祖父條款豁免，新產品一律擋掉。近期業界申請 3 倍與 5 倍槓桿 ETF，都被 SEC 以違反這條上限擋下。
3 倍槓桿 ETF 適合長期持有嗎？
不適合。這類產品每日重設曝險，在震盪行情中淨值會持續磨損。Volatility Shares 的 2 倍比特幣 ETF「BITX」今年跌 55.86%，同期比特幣僅跌 26.77%，倍數效果在下跌時會被放大。

title: Reddit 進標普 500 掀 1,670 萬股被動買盤，招股書上 BTC 持倉悄悄消失
summary:
標普道瓊指數公司週四（8/13）盤後宣布，Reddit（NYSE：RDDT）將於 8 月 18 日開盤前納入標 […]

〈Reddit 進標普 500 掀 1,670 萬股被動買盤，招股書上 BTC 持倉悄悄消失〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
標普道瓊指數公司週四（8/13）盤後宣布，Reddit（NYSE：RDDT）將於 8 月 18 日開盤前納入標普 500 指數，遞補被 Equity Residential 收購的 AvalonBay Communities。摩根大通估算被動基金得買進約 1,670 萬股，接近 Reddit 平均日成交量的三倍，股價週五盤中一度衝高 16.5%，收在 178.09 美元。動區查閱最新申報書發現，2024 年招股書寫進去的比特幣，如今已經不見蹤影。
（前情提要：Reddit申請IPO暴露「持倉BTC、ETH、MATIC..」，自家相關加密貨幣暴漲40%）
（背景補充：Reddit 宣布上鎖 API 與 old Reddit，想把開放論壇改成要門票的資料庫）
標普道瓊指數公司週四（8/13）盤後宣布，Reddit（NYSE：RDDT）將在 8 月 18 日開盤前納入標普 500 指數，遞補 AvalonBay Communities。後者正被同為成分股的 Equity Residential 收購，空出一個位子。
宣布之後，Reddit 股價週五（8/14）衝到盤中高點 184.28 美元，比前一天的 158.12 美元高出 16.5%，尾盤回吐一些，收在 178.09 美元，單日漲 12.63%。
真正的買盤還沒進場。摩根大通估算，追蹤指數的被動基金得吃下大約 1,670 萬股，接近 Reddit 自 2024 年 3 月掛牌以來平均日成交量 598 萬股的三倍。指數說要買，基金經理人沒有選擇權，這是被動投資時代的固定劇本。
虧了 20 年
標普 500 的入場條件在今年 6 月調整過：市值要 227 億美元以上，最近一季的 GAAP 獲利必須為正，最近連續四季合計也要為正。
Reddit 現在全部達標。6 月 30 日的在外流通股數是 Class A 1.458 億股加上 Class B 4,648 萬股，用 178.09 美元換算，市值約 342 億美元。第二季營收 8.049 億美元，年增 61%；淨利 2.528 億美元，去年同期只有 8,930 萬。日活躍用戶 1.303 億，年增 18%，每位用戶平均貢獻 6.18 美元，年增 36%。
動區 2024 年 11 月寫過它「20 年來首次盈利」，當時股價一天飆 50%。從第一次賺錢到湊滿四季獲利、擠進標普 500，它只花了兩年。Reddit 也是繼 Meta 之後，第二家進入標普 500 的純社群公司。
只是股價還沒補回年初的位置。以今年來算，RDDT 仍跌約 24%。
招股書上的比特幣不見了
這裡有件事值得加密讀者看一眼。
動區 2024 年 2 月報導過 Reddit 的 IPO 招股書，當時它自曝持有比特幣、以太幣與 Matic。招股書原文寫的是「我們將部分閒置現金投入比特幣與以太幣，另外以以太幣和 Matic 作為部分虛擬商品的收款方式」。
兩年後翻同一家公司的申報書，措辭變了。今年 2 月送出的 2025 年年報，以及 7 月 31 日送出的第二季季報，兩份都只剩一句話：「為了支援仰賴區塊鏈技術與 NFT 標準的業務，包括 Reddit Collectible Avatars，我們曾經取得並使用、也可能繼續取得並使用某些加密貨幣，包括以太幣與 Matic。」
比特幣在這兩份申報書裡是零次提及，「把閒置現金投進去」這種投資屬性的說法也一併消失，只剩業務用途。
要說得精確一點，財報不再提比特幣，不等於已經全部賣光，未達重大性門檻的部位本來就不一定要單獨列出。但至少可以確定，Reddit 已經不把持幣當成需要向股東交代的財務決策。

title: Weekend to bring significant drop in temperatures as heatwave ends
summary: Temperatures will tumble this weekend with the weather feeling noticeably cooler as the fifth widespread heatwave of the year comes to an end.
full_text:
Weekend to bring significant drop in temperatures as heatwave ends
- Published
Temperatures are set to tumble this weekend as the fifth heatwave to scorch the UK this year comes to an end.
After Thursday marked the hottest day of 2026 so far, conditions will be noticeably cooler on Saturday and Sunday.
Temperatures will fall by 10-15 degrees Celsius by the end of the weekend, bringing them much closer to the seasonal average.
The change in weather pattern that is bringing this cooler air will also result in an increased chance of rain, including in areas currently in drought.
Friday became the 39th day this year in which somewhere in the UK hit 30C (86F) or higher as the latest bout of extreme heat clung on in southern areas.
This smashed the previous UK record of 30 days set in 1995.
It was also only the ninth time since records began where a temperature of 37C (99F) or more has been registered.
Three of those occasions have been in 2026, sending a clear message that our climate is changing rapidly.
Dramatic drop in temperatures across the UK
The impact of the heat has been seen and felt in most aspects of daily life, from raging wildfires and transport delays to an increase in heat-related deaths, and for many the cooldown will be welcomed.
The change is being brought about by a cold front that has been moving south-eastwards through Friday and Friday night, introducing winds from a cooler north-westerly direction, as well as bringing a few showers.
While a few spots in south-east England could still reach their heatwave temperature threshold values of 27 or 28 Celsius on Saturday, many areas will be 10-13 degrees Celsius cooler than on Thursday.
Much of the UK, away from the south-east, will see highs of 16-24C.
These values are around average for mid-August but, given the exceptional heat experienced by many areas so far this summer, may feel comparatively cool.
Most areas will be dry with sunny spells, although a few showers are likely in north-west Scotland and East Anglia.
- UK sees hottest day of the year as 38.1C recorded in Kew Gardens 
  - Published1 day ago
Will there be more heatwaves this summer?
Most forecasts show that the cooler and more changeable spell of weather is set to continue for the rest of the month.
Some forecasts are also hinting at the potential for more significant rain-bearing low pressure systems tracking closer to the UK.
Temperatures are therefore more likely to stay closer to the seasonal average.
Some spells of warmer cannot be ruled out, especially in the south, but it looks unlikely at this time that further heatwaves will build this month.
While the meteorological summer comes to a close at the end of August it is not unusual for the UK for experience bouts of heat in September.

title: Sadie Sink and Adam Driver to star in new X-Men movie
summary: Heartstopper's Kit Connor and Christopher Abbot are also joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
full_text:
Sadie Sink and Adam Driver to star in new X-Men movie
- Published
Marvel Studios has announced a host of new actors for its X-Men reboot - including Stranger Things star Sadie Sink and Adam Driver.
The stars taking on the roles of seven characters in the new movie were unveiled at Disney's D23 fan event in the US on Friday.
Speaking at the event, Sink told the crowd it was "so wonderful" to be there and to "finally talk about the character after months of speculation"
Star Wars actor Driver joined via video-link as his character was revealed as the villainous Nathaniel Milbury, who will also been known as Mr Sinister.
The new X-Men film, which is currently untitled, will be directed by Jake Schreier and is out in cinemas in May 2028.
Sink will play Jean Grey, a character revealed to fans when she appeared in Spiderman: Brand New Day last month.
The other stars announced for X-Men were Heartstopper actor Kit Connor as Cyclops, Christopher Abbott as Professor Charles Xavier or X, Samara Weaving as Emma Frost, Inde Navarrette as Rogue and Maya Boyd as Storm.
Professor X has previously been played by Sir Patrick Stewart in other Marvel movies like Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.
Stewart will also appear as Professor X in the much-anticipated Avengers: Doomsday which is out later this year, before Abbott plays the role in X-Men.
Driver told fans at D23 he'd been talking "for years about maybe joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and I think we finally found the perfect film at the perfect time".
The last X-Men movie Dark Phoenix, which featured the likes of Jennifer Lawrence and Sophie Turner, came out in June 2019.
It was released under 20th Century Fox, but earlier that year, Disney, which owns Marvel, acquired the rights to the franchise.
Speaking at D23, Marvel Studios President Kevin Feige said there was a lot more X-Men casting news to come.

title: Tarling's team withdraws from Volta a Portugal after Briton's death
summary: Finlay Tarling's team, NSN, withdraws from the remaining stages of the Volta a Portugal following the British cyclist's death.
full_text:
Tarling's team withdraws as Volta a Portugal resumes
- Published
Finlay Tarling's team, NSN Development, have withdrawn from the remaining stages of the Volta a Portugal following the British cyclist's death.
The 19-year-old died following an accident during the eighth stage of the race on Friday.
Organisers confirmed the race will continue with the penultimate stage on Saturday, while tributes will be held for Tarling before the start.
In a statement, the Volta said it had been a "tragic day for cycling" and the race would be held in an "atmosphere of profound mourning".
It added that "as a sign of respect and mourning" the main sponsors of the event had agreed to cancel all activities for the remaining two stages.
"The race continues. There will be a sporting competition, but not a party... This Saturday, the Volta rides for Finlay."
Welshman Tarling was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8km route from Melgaco to Fafe on Friday.
In a statement provided to local media, Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said there had been "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle" and that an investigation was under way.
"Following Fin Tarling's tragic passing on Friday, the NSN Development Team has withdrawn from the remaining Volta a Portugal stages," NSN said in a statement on Saturday morning.
"With the full support of Fin's parents, the WorldTour team will race on at Czech Tour and the Arctic Race of Norway. We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts as we race in his honor, doing what he loved most.
"We want to thank everyone in the cycling community and beyond for the incredible support at this difficult time."
Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.
He looked to be following in the footsteps of his older brother Josh as a time trial specialist.
He finished in third in the under-23 men's individual time trial at the British Championships in June and competed in the Tour of Britain just under 12 months ago.
"This is not the time for speculation about the circumstances of the accident. The incident is being investigated by the GNR Command, which is responsible for rigorously establishing the facts," the Volta added.
"We all remain deeply shaken.
"Cycling is a sport that involves risks, but we are never prepared for a tragedy of this magnitude. Finlay lost his life. A family lost a son. A team lost a team-mate. Cycling lost one of its own. It is a tragedy that transcends the competition itself."

title: PSG sign World Cup final match-winner Torres from Barcelona
summary: Ferran Torres, who scored the winning goal for Spain at the World Cup, has joined European champions Paris St-Germain from Barcelona.
full_text:
PSG sign World Cup winner Torres from Barcelona
- Published
Ferran Torres, who scored the winning goal for Spain at the World Cup, has joined European champions Paris St-Germain from Barcelona.
The 26-year-old has signed a deal with the French champions until 2031 for a reported fee of about 50m euros (£42.7m).
He scored the extra-time winner against Argentina to help Spain claim their second men's World Cup last month, while his stock had already risen considerably after a strong season with Barcelona.
The forward scored 21 goals in 49 appearances in all competitions, providing three assists, and helped Barcelona win the La Liga title.
PSG, managed by former Barcelona coach and player Luis Enrique, have won the Champions League in the past two seasons.
Torres is the second high-profile forward PSG have signed this summer after the arrival of Maghnes Akliouche from Monaco.
PSG added to their silverware collection on Wednesday by beating Aston Villa 2-1 to win the Uefa Super Cup.
Torres has been at Barcelona since 2022 having previously spent two years at Manchester City.
He has scored 25 goals in 65 appearances for Spain and made his debut for the national team under Enrique.
PSG could lose Bradley Barcola this summer, with the forward wanted by Liverpool.

title: ICE detained a Venezuelan soccer pro. His case shows the immigration backlog crisis
summary: Homero Calderón's detention by ICE spotlights the massive backlog in the U.S. immigration system.
full_text:
ICE detained a Venezuelan soccer pro. His case shows the immigration backlog crisis
Homero Calderón used to spend his days training at the gym and on the soccer pitch. The professional soccer player built a long career, playing for clubs in Venezuela, Portugal, Cyprus and, most recently, Italy.
But for the last five months, Calderón has spent his days inside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in Folkston, Ga.
He's a father of two U.S. citizens, ages 1 and 3. Stuck in detention, his family says he's growing despondent. He recently missed his daughter's first birthday.
"I've been 17 years with Homero," his wife Daniela Molina said in a video published on social media. "I had never heard him cry or ask for help like he has."
Calderón was driving to a car shop in Florida in late February when he was pulled over for speeding by the Marion County Sheriff's Office and arrested for driving without a valid Florida license, the Department of Homeland Security told NPR in a statement. Molina said her husband had a valid international driving permit.
Calderón was eventually transferred to ICE custody. He's been in detention ever since.
In a statement to NPR, DHS said Calderón had "permission to stay until September 5, 2025" but that "he overstayed his welcome in violation of our nation's laws."
But Calderón was in the middle of two pending immigration cases when he was detained: he had applied on Aug. 25, 2025 for an extension of his tourist visa, and had also applied for a visa for people with extraordinary abilities. Called EB-1A visa, it allows people with extraordinary ability or achievement in fields including athletics, science, arts, education, and business to stay in the U.S. with a green card.
Neither open case kept him from being swept up in President Trump's immigration crackdown. His case represents a broader pattern, said Shev Dalal-Dheini, the senior director of government relations at the American Immigration Lawyers Association.
"His case is symbolic of so many other individuals who are stuck in processing backlogs at USCIS (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services) — individuals doing the right thing by filing their applications timely," Dalal-Dheini said. "But it's taking many, many, many months, if not in certain instances years, to have a case processed."
She believes the slow pace is by design.
"It's an easy way for the government to meet their quota to detain and deport individuals when they know who individuals are because they've done the right thing and applied for something," Dalal-Dheini said.
The backlog of cases at USCIS now stands at a staggering 11.3 million pending cases. The backlog was already high before President Trump took office, but since 2025 it has increased by more than 1.6 million cases, according to an analysis by the American Immigration Council.
And even though USCIS has received fewer immigration petitions, it also processed about 41% fewer cases at the beginning of the 2025 fiscal year, the group found.
"As the government takes longer to process applications, that means people are vulnerable to being arrested by ICE because they don't have a set status approved by the federal government," said Adriel Orozco, a senior policy counsel with the American Immigration Council.
According to Homero Calderón's family, the man has never committed a crime in the U.S. or in any other part of the world. NPR found no evidence of any past or pending criminal cases.
In the past, people like Calderón with pending USCIS applications or immigration court cases weren't priorities for detention.
"The government would allow those individuals to continue to follow that process," Orozco said, adding that going after them is "a waste of resources because at the end of the day, those individuals could be potentially approved for those statuses."
But Orozco says under the Trump administration that has shifted. Now every immigrant — despite the status of their immigration case — could be detained.
Waiting for his release
Ramón Calderón told NPR his brother Homero is disciplined, a skill honed after years of playing soccer professionally.
"When he was 2-years-old I remember when I used to play, he was running around the field," Ramón Calderón said.
At 16, Homero Calderón signed his first professional contract with Sport Club Guaraní in Venezuela, his brother said. Most of his career he's played midfield.
He last played professional soccer last year for the Italian team A.S.D. Arboris Belli 1979.
Throughout his life, his brother said, Homero Calderón has always followed the rules and laws no matter in which country he was.
That's what he did when he came to the U.S., Ramón Calderón said.
"He followed every single step of the process legally to obtain the legal status," he said.
Ramón Calderón himself is a U.S. citizen. He said his brother and mother have been coming to the U.S. since they were little kids. They never overstayed their visas, he said.
"We've done everything under the legality of what the immigration laws are," Ramón Calderón said. "So it's very, very hard and very difficult for our family to see him go through this nightmare."
It's unclear for how long Homero Calderón will remain in detention.
In a statement, DHS said Calderón will remain in ICE custody "pending the outcome of his immigration proceedings."
His brother hopes a resolution comes soon.
"We thought his case was strong, that we will get him out on bail and then follow his process and everything was going to be good there, but it's been six months," Ramón Calderón said. "We just need his process to have an answer, a final answer on his visa and his residency case. Whatever that result is going to be, we will accept."

full_text:
Why Chinese youth are turning to an 84-year-old Cambridge professor for support
To some of his 2.4 million followers, he is Grandpa Cute. Meet Alan Macfarlane, the gentle academic soothing China’s anxious generation
Wearing a black mariner’s cap and with a wall-to-wall bookshelf as a backdrop, Cambridge University professor Alan Macfarlane greets his social media audience with a soft ni hao – “Hello” in Chinese.
In his latest video, Macfarlane follows this signature opening by thoughtfully answering a question pulled from the comments: why has making genuine friends become so difficult?
Few would have expected an 84-year-old British anthropologist and historian from Cambridge University to become a social media heartthrob in China – yet Macfarlane has done exactly that.
Young Chinese affectionately call him “Grandpa Cute” or “Dumbledore”, after the beloved Harry Potter character, while his gentle, jargon-free reflections on education, purpose, anxiety, relationships, artificial intelligence (AI) and cultural understanding resonate deeply in a fast-paced, high-pressure society.
Through an intimate Q&A format, Macfarlane has amassed more than 2.4 million followers in roughly one year since launching on the Chinese social media platform RedNote in 2025, with videos often gaining millions of views.
His channels on Douyin – China’s version of TikTok – and Bilibili, another major video-sharing platform, have also attracted about 170,000 and 540,000 followers, respectively.

title: The Most Important Thing AI Can’t Do in Medicine
summary: Great physicians are curious about the patient in front of them, and that curiosity is what drives them to dig deeper, writes Dr. Natasha Chida.
full_text:
I was an early medical student at the University of Miami in Florida, seeing a patient in a local primary care clinic. “Abdominal pain with constipation,” I proudly told my supervising physician. “I think it’s irritable bowel syndrome.”
We went to see the patient and I watched with self-satisfaction as he asked the same questions I had. When did the pain start? Where is it? I waited for him to tell her it was likely IBS. But he didn’t. He paused and looked at her face after his last question, and for the first time I noticed she wasn’t making eye contact. She was looking at the ground. “We’ve known each other for a long time,” he told her gently, “and you seem worried. Can you share what you’re thinking?”
She didn’t say anything right away. Finally, she looked up. “My sister was just diagnosed with stage 4 colon cancer. I’m worried I might have it too.”
For the next 15 minutes I watched as they talked about how she was processing her sister’s diagnosis, her fears about the future, what it all meant for her future colon cancer screening, and why at this point we were most concerned about IBS.
By the end of the visit, her expression had cleared; I realized I hadn’t noticed how frightened she was. I felt ashamed of myself. What kind of doctor was I going to be?
My supervising physician and I talked about it. “You learn how to look,” he said. “When you care, you get a feel for it.”
You get a feel for it.
That lesson has stayed at the forefront for me as I’ve watched artificial intelligence sweep through medicine and enter the clinical environment of our internal medicine residency program at the Johns Hopkins Hospital. AI scribes. Chatbots that tell you a differential diagnosis if you put in a patient’s symptoms. Electronic medical record tools that will summarize a patient’s hospital course for you. But they can’t feel.
To be sure, AI can do incredible things in medicine. In this new world, I hear trainees wonder if AI will make doctors obsolete. I also hear some—usually not physicians—make this claim with confidence. They’re right about one thing: medicine is changing, and we in health care need to figure out our place in this new world.
But they’re wrong that physicians will become obsolete as AI becomes better at processing information. As I learned in medical school, truly caring for a patient begins before the first question is asked and the first test is ordered. It begins with looking. Noticing a second of hesitation before a patient responds. Seeing the pits in a nailbed. Hearing a change in heart sounds between visits. It begins when you commit to focusing entirely on the person in front of you, and to creating a relationship—that’s how you get a feel for it.
AI excels at processing information that is presented to it, like symptoms, test results, and even human expressions. It reasons with the input it is given. But it cannot decide what deserves attention before data exist.
Great physicians define the input. They decide which symptoms matter, observe what wasn’t said, and understand what information deserves the most attention. They are curious about the patient in front of them, and that curiosity drives them to dig deeper, discover information an algorithm couldn’t, and direct the flow of information—not just receive it.
Ironically, healthcare systems are already pushing physicians away from careful observation and curiosity toward the kind of medicine AI performs best: documenting, checking boxes, and following protocols. As a result, now many physicians don’t get the chance to experience the “feel” of medicine. Some ask questions (input) and tell the patient the plan (output)—but don’t observe or connect. They don’t have the time to practice the aspects of medicine that distinguish them from software.
Could AI in the coming decades replace these doctors? Probably. If the input is just data, the output would probably be the same. But the patients’ experience will be the one I would have given my patient with abdominal pain: incomplete and ineffective.
We need to embrace what AI can do to make medicine better while at the same time recognizing what it cannot do. We must see it for what it is—an adjunct to elevate physician care. A modern stethoscope.
Healthcare workers need to inform how medical AI is developed and deployed, so it doesn’t propagate checkbox medicine and promote the creation of AI-equivalent physicians who can follow protocols but have no feel for medicine.
We need to reimagine how we train the next generation of physicians, prioritizing the development of the skills and attributes needed to define the input—curiosity, careful observation, expert communication, and mastery of the physical exam—in the context of AI tools.
It also means we need to focus on recruiting people to medicine who have the “soft skills” and attributes that have defined great physicians for centuries: a focus on serving others, forming connections, building trust, and empathizing.
Years later, I remember little about the details of my patient’s abdominal pain. But I distinctly remember the moment she looked up after my supervising physician asked the question I never thought to ask.
AI will become better at recognizing disease. Whether medicine becomes better at recognizing patients depends on whether physicians still learn to look—and learn to feel.

title: Kalshi ordered to stop broad range of prediction markets in Washington
summary: Kalshi must implement initial geofencing by Aug. 19 and a GeoComply multi-source geofencing system by Sept. 2.
full_text:
Kalshi ordered to stop broad range of prediction markets in Washington
Kalshi must implement initial geofencing by Aug. 19 and a GeoComply multi-source geofencing system by Sept. 2.
A Washington state judge has ordered prediction market platform Kalshi to stop offering a broad range of event contracts in the state, rejecting its argument that federal commodities law preempts Washington gambling law.
King County Superior Court Judge John McHale barred Kalshi from offering contracts tied to sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, and “mentions.” Contracts involving commodities, climate, economics and finance are exempt.
“We’re holding Kalshi accountable for running an illegal gambling operation,” Washington Attorney General Nick Brown said Thursday on X, citing a recent court ruling.
Kalshi must implement IP-address and residency-based geofencing by Aug. 19 and a GeoComply multi-source geofencing system by Sept. 2 to prevent people in Washington from purchasing contracts covered by the injunction.
The amended order, signed Wednesday, sets the terms of a preliminary injunction McHale granted in July. The judge found that the Commodity Exchange Act does not preempt Washington gambling law and that the state had shown a likelihood of success on claims under three state laws.
Kalshi maintains that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over its exchange. The Washington Court of Appeals denied its request to stay the injunction.

title: This Beautifully Weird Necklace Is Secretly a USB Drive
summary: Noware’s Puff necklace whimsically reimagines flash drives, turning something functional into personalized jewelry.
full_text:
I’m already growing hoarse in Golden Gate Park as Charli XCX takes the stage at a San Francisco music festival. The crowd starts jumping as a guitar hook hits, and I reluctantly comply, bouncing around on these aging knees as my chunky Puff necklace almost flies off the chain.
During a lull in the set, someone next to me compliments the necklace, which has stainless steel swirls and a bulbous orange center. Their eyes grow wide as I flip the cap off and explain that it’s a hidden USB flash drive—I plugged the Puff into my phone to show off the animations.
When Harry Isaac and Sebastian Bidegain, working together under the Noware moniker, posted an early prototype of their retro-futuristic necklace on social media in 2025, it quickly racked up over a million views with thousands of waitlist sign-ups to buy one. The duo has spent the last year attempting to turn the online attention on their prototype into a mass-produced reality. Now, Noware is finally ready to ship units this October.
The pair arrived at the WIRED office wearing Puff necklaces, naturally, that match with their trendy gorpcore outfits. They seem nervous, albeit excited, to show off their creation. Neither has had a wide release for their products before, though both are well-versed in whimsical designs. Isaac previously went viral for making an electric scooter that shoots out bubbles. Bidegain was already sculpturally approaching electronics, with prototypes like a vape camera and lo-fi sampler built into a rock.
The design ethos of the Puff is just as much about aesthetics as it is about usefulness. Noware’s marketing materials show a cool girl with a Puff clipped onto her purse, where a Labubu might have sat last year, as well as styled on her neck with a pile of other silver chains. Bidegain says the “squishy, doughy” textures of food partially inspired Puff’s design, as well as cellular biology and tactile devices, like old phones and radios.
“On one end, I want anyone to be able to wear it, just if they think it's pretty,” he says. “Though, I also want people who actually find utility in flash drives as part of their workflow: photographers, DJs, IT people.”
The small screen in the middle of the necklace is my favorite aspect. When it’s plugged into my phone or laptop, Puff’s center lights up with a customizable design. The Noware duo showed me goopy animations that reacted to the direction I held the phone as well as an aquarium mode. They even put the WIRED logo on it through custom software anyone can use to craft their own designs. The Puff doesn’t have an internal battery, so the USB drive can live as a piece of jewelry far longer than the expiration date of most electronics.
The necklace’s biggest drawback is its price: a whopping $179 for only 128 GB of storage. A basic flash drive with similar storage costs around $30. The duo doesn’t want the Puff to remain that expensive and hopes to reach a more accessible price. “We want it to get cheaper over time, but we're just trying to make it exist first,” says Isaac. They blame it partially on the inflated cost of memory right now, thanks to the AI boom. Depending on how Puff’s initial release goes, future iterations may include more budget-friendly options, like a nonmetal version.
This experimental device from two New York City-based makers was the perfect accessory for a weekend-long festival, with its retro-futuristic vibe and sharp colors.
“We're very interested in making electronics that are more opinionated, playful, and personal,” Isaac says. It was a lighthearted conversation piece as I made small talk with vendors, and at least one friend assumed I was hiding drugs in it. (Nope, just a bunch of nudes.)

title: Retrospec Joe Rev 2 Review (2026): Putting the ‘Joy’ in Joyride
summary: This affordable electric BMX delighted my entire family, even if its range, ride comfort, and actual BMX abilities are limited.
full_text:
Fun, retro style that appeals to both teens and adults. Well-priced. UL-2271 and 2849 certified. Frame triangle is big enough to attach a folding lock.
TIRED
Seat is cheap-feeling and very hard. No suspension and no way to carry cargo. Range takes a huge hit on hills. No battery IP rating for water resistance. Not a “real” BMX.
Though I’ve since gotten used to it, every time I ride the electric blue Joe Rev 2 electric BMX, people stare. Their heads turn as they drive past, eyes narrowed. “Is that an adult riding a BMX bike?” I imagine the thought process going. “Why is it so fast? Why is it so big?” These are valid questions, and they all have the same answer: Because it’s fun.
In fact, my entire family has taken turns riding this bike all over town for the past four weeks, testing it up and down hills, taking it on grocery runs, and even staying out riding until the battery drained. The verdict? The Joe Rev 2 may not be the smoothest ride, but for the price, it’s a unique and worthwhile option for basic cruising and casual riding.
All Eyes on Me
Photograph: Kat Merck
California-based Retrospec specializes in affordable outdoor toys; primarily paddleboards, longboards, bikes, and no-frills ebikes like the foldable Judd Rev 2, which WIRED contributing reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani wrote “captures the vibe of being a 12-year-old kid and riding your bike more than anything I’ve ridden in some time.”
The entry-level Joe Rev was created in this same spirit—a full-sized, BMX-inspired frame with fun color options (electric blue, matte gray), 3-inch tan wall balloon tires, and those unmistakable handlebars. There are no apps or fancy readouts, no lights, and no shocks. Just five levels of pedal assist and a throttle attached to a single-speed drivetrain and 750-watt rear-hub motor.
Photograph: Kat Merck
“No cream, no sugar” is even printed on the chain stays, lest one forget the minimalist doctrine. On the plus side, this lack of bones allows the Joe Rev 2 to weigh in on the lighter side at 56 pounds.
This is the second iteration of the original Joe Rev, which is still available (for now) at the sale price of $1,200. The Rev 2 sports a bigger 500 Wh battery with a listed 60-mile range (up from 48 miles) and an updated display. Namely, a 2-by-2.5-inch LCD screen on the left handlebar displaying power level, battery life, and speed, as opposed to the original’s bare-basic hub with buttons.
The battery can be quickly locked and unlocked from the bottom of the frame with a key and charges from red to full green in several hours; it weighs about 7 pounds, so it’s easy enough to carry in a backpack, though at 18 inches long, it could be a tight fit if your bag is already packed.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
Teen Spirit
At one point during the testing period, my almost-14-year-old son, who is 5’ 10” and 145 pounds, took the Joe Rev 2 out on a full battery to see how long he could ride in our town of hills. We were all surprised to find he hit the red “recharge” light in about 20 miles. It shouldn't have been too much of a shock, given that the hills were steep, and he was using the throttle primarily. But it is a good reminder that, like all ebikes, the Joe Rev 2’s range will vary dramatically depending on rider weight, speed, and conditions.
Interestingly, there’s an ominous warning sticker on the Joe Rev’s frame that states no one under 16 is to ride this bike. It does have pedals and a maximum speed of 20 mph, making it a Class 2 ebike—legal in many, if not, most states for kids under 16.
When I asked Retrospec if there was anything specific about the Joe Rev 2 that would preclude younger teens from riding it, their rep told me the company “follows the most stringent regulations across the markets where their ebikes are sold. As a result, their minimum recommended rider age is 16. If local laws permit younger riders, such as a 12-year-old, it is ultimately up to parents or guardians to determine whether their child has the maturity, experience, and ability to safely operate an ebike.”
However, an adult-sized, mature 14- or 15-year-old could be a gray area. My son is allowed to ride the Joe Rev 2 occasionally, but not regularly. If you decide to go this route, know this bike was deemed acceptable by several teens in my orbit, though stylistically a couple notches below the e-moto-style frames popularized by brands like MacFox.
How It Rides
As is typical with ebikes, some assembly of the Joe Rev 2 is required upon arrival. Chiefly, attaching the wheels, pedals, and handlebars, for which it comes with a generously sized set of hex wrenches. The first night, it took a couple of tries to get the front wheel seated properly—there was a slight wobble during my husband’s inaugural ride around the block, but after further tightening, it has not resurfaced. The brakes are mechanical disc with 180 mm rotors, which also occasionally needed tightening, but otherwise caused no issues during the testing period.
My own first ride was on a flat surface, around the parking lot of my son’s former elementary school. I found that the five levels of pedal assist kick in quickly and almost forcefully; the throttle is an easy-to-use thumb switch located on the left handlebar. The frame feels like a good size for my height (5’ 6”), and the whole setup was easy to parse in just a couple of minutes.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Aside from the lack of suspension—you will feel every bump—my only major complaint is the seat. In fact, my butt still hurts as I write this from even a short ride yesterday. The Joe Rev 2's seat is hard, plasticky, and small—definitely worth swapping out if you’re going to be commuting on this or otherwise riding it daily.
My 5’ 8” husband rides the Joe Rev 2 to the grocery store several times a week, an activity he greatly enjoys, and over time we’ve found ourselves wishing there were an easy way to carry cargo, such as the ability to bolt on a basket or saddlebags. To be fair, though, I’m not sure it would ultimately be worth the reduction in range, though the bike does have a payload capacity of 350 pounds. We do, however, greatly appreciate the open space in the frame to attach a folding lock. (We went with the Seatlylock FoldyLock for $90).
One thing I have not yet been able to test is the water resistance. I live in western Washington state, where it rains nine months out of the year, and the Joe Rev 2's battery is mounted at the bottom of the down tube, where it could easily be splashed. There's no given IP rating for water resistance, so while I'm sure the battery housing can handle a light, occasional spray, riding the bike on a super-rainy day would make me nervous.
It also bears mentioning that if you're hoping for a real BMX bike with which you can do tricks, the Joe Rev 2 is not that. Insofar as being a BMX, the only quality seems to be the handlebars. Nothing about it feels nimble, and at this weight, you’re not taking it to the skate park—the only jumps and rail hops happening are in your imagination.
However, if you do happen to lose control of yourself and break something, the Joe Rev 2 is UL 2849 Certified for the electrical system and UL 2271 Certified for the battery, meaning that, unlike with many other internet-purchased direct-to-consumer bikes, your local bike shop may be able to repair it. Though this depends heavily on the type of repair needed; it’s worth calling to be sure.
Kat Merck is a commerce editor for WIRED, where she covers smart bird feeders, indoor gardening systems, kitchen composters, and all things sustainable home tech.
